subject: history
subTopic: The Treaty of Versailles and Its Effects

questions.content: In which year was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
questions.explanation: The armistice was in November 1918, but the treaty was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 28 June 1919. The reparations total was fixed later, in 1921.

questions.content: What was Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, often called?
questions.explanation: Article 231 made Germany and its allies accept responsibility for the damage of the war, the legal basis for reparations.

questions.content: How large was the German army allowed to be under the Treaty of Versailles?
questions.explanation: The army was limited to 100,000 volunteers, with no conscription, tanks or air force.

questions.content: Who were the 'Big Three' leaders at the Paris Peace Conference?
questions.explanation: They led the United States, Britain and France. Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin were the Big Three of the Second World War.

questions.content: What was the purpose of the League of Nations, set up after the First World War?
options: To keep peace through collective security and negotiation
To rule the former German colonies as its own territory
questions.explanation: Members would settle disputes peacefully and act together against an aggressor, though the League had no army of its own.

questions.content: Why did many Germans call the Treaty of Versailles a 'Diktat'?
options: Germany was not allowed to negotiate and had to accept the terms
questions.explanation: 'Diktat' means dictated peace. German delegates saw the terms only when they were presented and were threatened with renewed war if they refused.

questions.content: Which Allied leader pushed hardest for a harsh settlement to weaken Germany and protect France?
questions.explanation: France had suffered invasion twice in fifty years, so Clemenceau wanted Germany weakened. Wilson argued for self-determination and a League of Nations.

questions.content: In 1921 reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks. If Germany had paid 2 billion gold marks every year, how many years would it have taken to pay in full?
questions.explanation: 132 ÷ 2 = 66. The size of the debt helps explain German resentment and why the schedule was later revised, for example by the Young Plan.

questions.content: Which territory was returned to France under the Treaty of Versailles?
questions.explanation: Alsace-Lorraine had been taken by Germany in 1871. The Saar was put under League administration for 15 years, and the Sudetenland was never German before 1938.

questions.content: Why did France and Belgium occupy the Ruhr in January 1923?
options: Germany had fallen behind on reparations deliveries
The Weimar government had asked for help
The League of Nations ordered Germany's disarmament
questions.explanation: Germany had missed payments in coal and timber, so the occupying troops seized industrial output. German workers' passive resistance and money printing led to hyperinflation.

questions.content: What did the Dawes Plan of 1924 do?
options: Reorganised reparations payments and arranged American loans to Germany
questions.explanation: The Dawes Plan eased payments and brought in US loans, helping Germany recover, but it also made Germany dependent on American money.

questions.content: An invented German newspaper headline from 1919 reads: 'A shameful chain, not a peace.' What does this suggest about the treaty?
options: Many Germans saw it as unjust and resented it
questions.explanation: The headline shows anger at the treaty, though one newspaper does not show all opinion, and the press had its own political stance.

questions.content: What did Germany accept in the Locarno Treaties of 1925?
options: Its western borders with France and Belgium and the demilitarised Rhineland
A limit of 100,000 on its navy only
questions.explanation: Locarno, helped by Stresemann, eased tension and led to Germany joining the League of Nations in 1926. Germany did not accept its eastern borders.

questions.content: Which argument supports the view that the Treaty of Versailles was NOT as harsh as many Germans claimed?
options: Germany stayed united with its industry intact, and its own 1918 treaty with Russia (Brest-Litovsk) had been harsher
The army was limited to 100,000 men
Germany was blamed for the war
Germany was not invited to the negotiations
questions.explanation: The other options are arguments that support harshness. Germany remained a major power with its core industry, and at Brest-Litovsk it had taken large areas from Russia.

questions.content: Why did some Germans actually benefit from the hyperinflation of 1923?
options: Savers and pensioners saw their wealth grow
Wages stayed fixed and rose in value
Those with large debts or mortgages could repay them with worthless money
questions.explanation: When money loses its value, fixed debts become easy to pay off. Savers and people on fixed incomes lost the most.

questions.content: A fictional loaf of bread cost 250 marks in January 1923 and 200 billion marks in November 1923. By what factor did the price rise?
questions.explanation: 200,000,000,000 ÷ 250 = 800,000,000. Such a rise destroyed savings and trust in the Weimar government.

questions.content: How did the Treaty of Versailles damage the Weimar Republic politically?
options: Politicians who signed it were blamed as 'November criminals', feeding the myth that Germany had been stabbed in the back
It gave the army control of the government
It made Germany a monarchy again
questions.explanation: Nationalists claimed the army had not been defeated and that civilians betrayed it, undermining the democratic government.

questions.content: Which example shows the principle of self-determination being applied inconsistently at Versailles?
options: Germany was forced to pay reparations
Austria was forbidden to unite with Germany, and millions of German-speakers were placed in Czechoslovakia and Poland
questions.explanation: Wilson's idea that peoples should choose their own governments was not applied to Germans in Austria, the Sudetenland or Poland, which Hitler later exploited.

note:
## The settlement
The First World War ended with an armistice on 11 November 1918. The peace treaties were then drawn up in Paris in 1919 by the victors. The 'Big Three' were Woodrow Wilson (USA), David Lloyd George (Britain) and Georges Clemenceau (France). Germany was not allowed to take part in the negotiations and was told to sign the Treaty of Versailles on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors.

## Competing aims
- **Wilson** wanted a fair peace based on his Fourteen Points, including self-determination and a League of Nations.
- **Clemenceau** wanted to cripple Germany to protect France, which had been invaded twice.
- **Lloyd George** wanted to punish Germany but not so harshly that it would want revenge, and he wanted trade to recover.

## The main terms
- **War guilt (Article 231)**: Germany accepted blame for the war.
- **Reparations**: fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks.
- **Disarmament**: army limited to 100,000 men, no conscription, tanks or air force, navy limited with no submarines.
- **Territory**: Alsace-Lorraine to France; land to Poland, including the Polish Corridor; the Saar under League control for 15 years; Germany lost its colonies as League mandates. Overall Germany lost about 13% of its land.
- **Rhineland** demilitarised, with Allied occupation.
- **Anschluss** (union with Austria) was forbidden.

## Effects in Germany
Most Germans hated the treaty, calling it a 'Diktat', and politicians who signed were blamed as 'November criminals'. In January 1923 France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr when reparations were late. Workers went on strike, the government printed money and **hyperinflation** wiped out savings, though people with debts gained. Under Gustav Stresemann the currency was replaced by the Rentenmark. The **Dawes Plan (1924)** reorganised payments with US loans, **Locarno (1925)** secured Germany's western borders, Germany joined the League in 1926 and the **Young Plan (1929)** reduced and extended the payments. Recovery depended on American money, so it was fragile.

## Other treaties
The Allies signed separate treaties with the other defeated powers: Saint-Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria) and, with Turkey, Sèvres, replaced by Lausanne in 1923.

## Common mistakes
- Saying the treaty ended German unity. Germany survived as one state and kept its industry.
- Mixing up the dates: armistice 1918, treaty 1919, reparations total fixed 1921, Ruhr occupation 1923.
- Treating the treaty as simply harsh or simply fair. Historians debate this, so give evidence on both sides, for example that Germany stayed united and kept its industry, yet lost land, its colonies and its freedom to rearm.

## How this is examined
You might be given a source, such as a German cartoon or British newspaper comment from 1919, and asked to explain its origin and purpose, then judge how far the treaty caused later problems. A data question might ask you to interpret reparations or inflation figures.

Exam tip: for 'how far' questions, compare at least two factors, such as the treaty and the Depression, and conclude which mattered more and why.

flashcards.back: Signed 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors. Imposed on Germany: war guilt, reparations, disarmament, territorial losses.
The War Guilt Clause: Germany had to accept responsibility for the war, the basis for reparations.
Payments for war damage. Total fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks.
Army limited to 100,000 volunteers; no tanks, air force or conscription; navy restricted with no submarines; Rhineland demilitarised.
Wilson: fair peace, self-determination, League. Clemenceau: cripple Germany. Lloyd George: punish but avoid revenge, restore trade.
German word for a dictated peace: Germany was not allowed to negotiate the Treaty of Versailles.
France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr when reparations were late; strikes and money printing led to hyperinflation.
Reorganised reparations and brought American loans, helping German recovery but making Germany dependent on US money.
Germany accepted its western borders with France and Belgium; Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926.

subject: history

questions.content: In which month and year did the Wall Street Crash begin?
questions.explanation: Share prices collapsed from 24 October 1929 ('Black Thursday') and fell further on 29 October.

questions.content: Who was elected US President in 1932 and began the New Deal?
questions.explanation: Roosevelt defeated Hoover in November 1932 and took office in March 1933.

questions.content: What does 'buying on the margin' mean?
options: Borrowing money to buy shares, hoping prices will rise
questions.explanation: If prices fell, buyers could not repay their loans, which helped turn the Crash into a banking crisis.

questions.content: What were 'Hoovervilles'?
options: Shanty towns built by the homeless and unemployed
questions.explanation: They were named ironically after President Hoover, whom many blamed for failing to help.

questions.content: By 1933, about what proportion of the US workforce was unemployed?
questions.explanation: Unemployment reached around 25% at its worst, with millions of families in hardship.

questions.content: Why did the Wall Street Crash cause a worldwide depression?
options: American banks recalled loans from Europe, especially Germany, and world trade collapsed
The League of Nations closed the banks
questions.explanation: Countries such as Germany had relied on US loans. When these were withdrawn, factories closed and unemployment rose.

questions.content: What was the effect of the US Hawley-Smoot Tariff of 1930?
options: Higher taxes on imports led other countries to retaliate, reducing world trade
It lowered import taxes and increased trade
It paid farmers to produce more
questions.explanation: The tariff aimed to protect US industry but contributed to a collapse in international trade.

questions.content: In a fictional town, unemployment rose from 2,000 workers in 1929 to 9,000 in 1932. What is the percentage increase?
What was the purpose of the 1933 bank holiday and Emergency Banking Act?
options: To close the banks, inspect them and reopen only sound ones to restore confidence
questions.explanation: Roosevelt acted in his first days to stop the panic of people withdrawing their savings.

questions.content: Which New Deal agency employed young men on conservation projects such as planting trees?
questions.explanation: The CCC gave jobs and a wage to unemployed young men. The TVA built dams and brought electricity to one poor region.

questions.content: What was the Jarrow March of 1936?
options: A strike of coal miners in Wales
A march of soldiers returning from Spain
A march of unemployed men from a northern English town to London to ask for work after the shipyard closed
questions.explanation: It became a symbol of unemployment in Britain's industrial north in the 1930s.

questions.content: The Nazi Party won about 2.6% of the vote in May 1928 and about 37.3% in July 1932. Which explanation fits best?
options: Mass unemployment and anger with the government turned voters to extreme parties
questions.explanation: The Depression hit Germany severely when US loans were withdrawn, and many voters were attracted by the Nazis' promises of jobs and national pride.

questions.content: An invented photograph description shows tar-paper shacks beside a river and men queuing for soup. What is the main limitation of this as evidence of the Depression?
options: It is worthless because photos can lie
It is reliable because photographs never mislead
It shows only one scene chosen by the photographer, so it may not represent everywhere
It was taken after the Depression
questions.explanation: A photograph shows real hardship but captures one place at one time and was framed deliberately. It should be combined with other evidence.

questions.content: Which weakness of the 1920s US economy made the Crash more damaging?
options: Wealth was unequal and ordinary people could not afford all the goods being produced
questions.explanation: Overproduction and falling consumer demand combined with speculation and weak bank regulation to create a fragile economy.

questions.content: Which evidence best supports the view that the New Deal alone did not end the Depression?
options: Unemployment was still high at the end of the 1930s and fell sharply only with wartime production
questions.explanation: The recovery was only partial, and rearmament and war production brought unemployment down.

questions.content: Why did the Supreme Court strike down parts of the New Deal, such as the NRA and the AAA?
options: It ruled that they gave the federal government powers beyond those in the Constitution
It wanted to end the Depression
questions.explanation: Opponents argued the New Deal expanded federal power too far, and Roosevelt later tried to change the Court's makeup, which was controversial.

questions.content: Which idea linked to the economist John Maynard Keynes influenced responses to the Depression?
options: Governments should cut spending in every slump
Governments should spend to boost demand in a slump, even by borrowing
questions.explanation: Keynes argued that when private spending collapses, public spending can create jobs and restart the economy.

questions.content: Which reason best explains why extremist parties gained far less support in Britain than in Germany?
options: Britain had stable democratic institutions and had not suffered defeat, hyperinflation and a hated peace, while Germany's democracy was new and fragile
questions.explanation: Depression hit both countries, but German democracy had weak roots and was blamed for national humiliation.

note:
## Boom and crash
In the 1920s the United States boomed. Many people bought shares, often 'on the margin' by borrowing money. Factories made more goods than people could afford, farmers faced falling prices and wealth was unequally shared. On 24 October 1929 ('Black Thursday') share prices collapsed and panic selling followed on 29 October. Banks that had lent money failed, and ordinary savers lost their money.

## A worldwide depression
The Crash did not cause everything, but it triggered a global crisis. American banks recalled loans from Europe. Germany, which relied heavily on US loans under the Dawes Plan, was hit hard. The US Hawley-Smoot Tariff (1930) raised import taxes, other countries retaliated, and world trade collapsed. Industries closed, wages fell and unemployment soared: about a quarter of US workers by 1933, around 6 million in Germany in 1932 and about 3 million in Britain.

## Responses in the USA
President Hoover believed that government should not interfere much and that the economy would recover. By 1932 millions were homeless, living in 'Hoovervilles'. Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 election promising a **New Deal**. In his first Hundred Days he closed the banks to restore confidence, then created many agencies:
- **CCC**: work for young men on conservation.
- **AAA**: paid farmers to reduce output and raise prices.
- **TVA**: dams and cheap electricity in a poor region.
- **Social Security Act (1935)**: pensions and unemployment insurance.
Critics on the right said Roosevelt gave government too much power, and the Supreme Court struck down parts of the New Deal. Others said it did not go far enough. Unemployment stayed high until war production boosted the economy.

## Responses elsewhere
In Britain the National Government (1931) cut spending, left the gold standard and raised tariffs. In 1936 unemployed men from Jarrow marched to London. Democracy survived. In Germany the Depression ended the Weimar Republic's fragile stability, as voters turned to the Nazis and Communists. In Japan the crisis encouraged the military to seek an empire, including the invasion of Manchuria in 1931.

## Common mistakes
- Saying the Crash was the only cause of the Depression; weaknesses already existed.
- Claiming the New Deal ended the Depression on its own.
- Forgetting the political effects: the Depression helped extremists rise in Germany and Japan.

## How this is examined
Questions may give you unemployment figures or election results as plain-text data and ask you to calculate a change, identify a trend and explain it with your own knowledge. You may also be asked to evaluate a photograph or poster, stating its origin, purpose, value and limitation.

Exam tip: when you use statistics, say what they show, give one reason for the trend, and note a limit, such as unemployment figures being estimates that count people differently.

flashcards.back: Collapse of US share prices from 24 October 1929 ('Black Thursday'), followed by bank failures and a worldwide depression.
Borrowing money to buy shares, hoping prices will rise. When they fell, borrowers and banks were ruined.
US import taxes raised sharply; other countries retaliated and world trade collapsed.
It relied on US loans (Dawes Plan). When they were recalled, unemployment reached about 6 million in 1932.
Shanty town of the homeless and unemployed, named bitterly after President Hoover.
Roosevelt's programme from 1933: bank rescue, work schemes (CCC), farm help (AAA), TVA, Social Security (1935).
Unemployment stayed high until wartime production; the Supreme Court struck down parts; critics said too much or too little.
National Government 1931, spending cuts, left gold standard; Jarrow March 1936. Democracy survived.
Mass unemployment helped the Nazis rise in Germany (37.3% in July 1932) and encouraged Japanese militarism and expansion.

subject: history

questions.content: Who led the Italian Fascists to power in 1922?
questions.explanation: Benito Mussolini founded the Fascist movement in 1919 and became Prime Minister in October 1922.

questions.content: What was the result of the March on Rome in October 1922?
options: King Victor Emmanuel III invited Mussolini to form a government
questions.explanation: Fascist threats of force persuaded the king not to resist, and Mussolini became Prime Minister legally, then built a dictatorship.

questions.content: What title did Hitler take after President Hindenburg died in August 1934?
questions.explanation: Hitler combined the offices of Chancellor and President and called himself Führer (leader).

questions.content: Whom did the Nazis blame for the Reichstag Fire of February 1933?
questions.explanation: A Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was arrested and the Nazis used the fire to claim a communist plot.

questions.content: What did the name of Hitler's party, the NSDAP, stand for?
questions.explanation: The Nazi Party was a nationalist and racist party, despite using the word 'socialist'.

questions.content: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 allow?
options: Hitler's government to make laws without the Reichstag for four years
The end of the Nazi Party
questions.explanation: After the Reichstag Fire Decree, the Reichstag voted by the required majority to hand its powers to the government.

questions.content: Why did Hitler order the Night of the Long Knives in June–July 1934?
options: To remove the SA leadership under Röhm and rivals, and win the army's support
To start a war with Austria
questions.explanation: The SA's size and radicalism worried the army, so Hitler killed Röhm and others, reassuring generals.

questions.content: The Nazi vote share was 37.3% in July 1932 and 33.1% in November 1932. By how many percentage points did it fall?
questions.explanation: 37.3 − 33.1 = 4.2. The Nazis were still the largest party, but they never won a majority in a free election.

questions.content: Which was a method Mussolini used to build a dictatorship?
options: Banning other political parties and controlling the press
questions.explanation: By 1925–26 he had banned opposition parties, censored newspapers and used secret police such as the OVRA.

questions.content: What did the Nuremberg Laws of September 1935 do?
options: Removed German citizenship from Jews and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews
questions.explanation: They defined Jews by ancestry and made persecution part of the law.

questions.content: Why did the Nazis promote cheap radios, the 'People's Receivers'?
options: To spread propaganda to as many homes as possible
questions.explanation: Goebbels, as Minister of Propaganda, used radio, film, rallies and newspapers to control information.

questions.content: An invented description of a 1930s rally poster shows thousands of people in perfect rows beneath huge banners, with one figure on a platform. What is its likely purpose?
options: To give an accurate record of normal life
To show strength, unity and obedience, impressing supporters and intimidating opponents
questions.explanation: The poster is propaganda, created to present an image of order and loyalty, so it should not be taken as proof of real opinion.

questions.content: Which features did Italian Fascism and Nazism share?
options: A one-party state, extreme nationalism, a leader cult and violence against opponents
questions.explanation: Both were totalitarian movements, although Nazism put racial ideas at its centre.

questions.content: Why did President Hindenburg appoint Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933?
options: Hitler had won an outright majority
Conservatives such as von Papen believed they could control him and use his mass support
questions.explanation: The Nazis were the largest party but without a majority. The conservatives thought they would be the real power behind Hitler, and were wrong.

questions.content: Which statement correctly contrasts Nazism with Soviet communism?
options: Nazism kept private business under state direction and stressed race, while communism abolished private ownership and stressed class
questions.explanation: Both were dictatorships that used terror, but their ideas and economic systems differed.

questions.content: Which statement gives the best-balanced explanation of how Hitler kept control after 1933?
options: He combined terror and propaganda with genuine popularity from jobs and foreign policy successes
questions.explanation: Control rested on fear (Gestapo, camps), propaganda and consent, because many people were pleased with falling unemployment and the restoration of German pride.

questions.content: Why was the Reichstag Fire Decree of February 1933 so important to the Nazis?
options: It gave Hitler the title Führer
It suspended civil liberties, allowing arrests of Communists and opponents before the March election
questions.explanation: The decree ended freedom of speech and assembly, allowing the Nazis to campaign with an advantage.

questions.content: What did the policy of 'Gleichschaltung' (coordination) aim to do?
options: Bring state governments, trade unions, the press and clubs under Nazi control
questions.explanation: It removed independent organisations in the 1930s so that society followed Nazi direction.

note:
## What is fascism?
Fascism emerged after the First World War, when many Europeans feared communism, were angry about peace settlements and were hit by economic crisis. Fascist movements were extremely nationalist, anti-communist and anti-democratic. They glorified the nation and the leader, praised violence and aimed to control all parts of life, which is **totalitarianism**.

## Mussolini's Italy
Benito Mussolini founded the Fascist movement in 1919. Italy had suffered heavy losses in the war and felt cheated by the peace treaties, while unemployment and strikes frightened the middle class. In October 1922 the Fascists staged the **March on Rome**. King Victor Emmanuel III chose not to resist and asked Mussolini to form a government. By 1925–26 Mussolini ruled as **Il Duce**: opposition parties were banned, newspapers were censored, a secret police (OVRA) operated, and propaganda promoted his cult. In 1929 the Lateran Treaty with the Pope won Catholic support. He invaded Abyssinia in 1935.

## Hitler's rise
Hitler led the Nazi Party (NSDAP). After the failed Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch of November 1923 he went to prison, wrote *Mein Kampf* and decided to win power legally. The party grew little until the Great Depression: from 2.6% of votes in 1928 to 37.3% in July 1932, when it became the largest party. It never won a majority in a free election. On 30 January 1933 President Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor, as conservatives like von Papen believed they could control him.

## Building the dictatorship
- **27 February 1933**: Reichstag Fire. A decree suspended civil liberties.
- **23 March 1933**: Enabling Act let Hitler make laws without the Reichstag.
- **Gleichschaltung**: other parties, trade unions and state governments were brought under Nazi control.
- **30 June–2 July 1934**: Night of the Long Knives. Röhm and other SA leaders were killed, winning army support.
- **August 1934**: Hindenburg died and Hitler became Führer.
Control used terror (SS, Gestapo, camps), propaganda (Goebbels, radio, rallies, Hitler Youth) and benefits such as falling unemployment. Persecution of Jews was legal: the **Nuremberg Laws** (1935) removed their citizenship, and violence grew in the Kristallnacht pogrom of 9–10 November 1938.

## Common mistakes
- Saying Hitler won a majority in a free election; he did not.
- Saying the Nazis seized power by force alone. Legal appointment, Enabling Act and intimidation all mattered.
- Mixing up Hitler's Führer with Mussolini's Duce.

## How this is examined
Expect a source such as a Nazi poster, rally photograph or election table, and tasks to state its origin, purpose, value and limitation, or to explain how a dictator consolidated power using the source and your own knowledge.

Exam tip: when writing about how a dictator gained power, separate the conditions (economic crisis, weak democracy) from the methods (legal manoeuvres, propaganda, terror) and link them in your answer.

flashcards.back: Extreme nationalist, anti-communist, anti-democratic ideology led by a dictator, with a one-party state, a leader cult and violence.
Fascist show of force; King Victor Emmanuel III asked Mussolini to form a government. He became Il Duce by 1925–26.
Hitler's failed attempt to seize power in November 1923. He was jailed, wrote Mein Kampf and chose to seek power legally.
2.6% in 1928, 37.3% in July 1932 (largest party), 33.1% in November 1932. Never a majority in free elections.
Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor; conservatives such as von Papen believed they could control him.
27 Feb 1933 fire led to a decree suspending civil liberties; the Act of 23 March 1933 let Hitler make laws without the Reichstag.
30 June–2 July 1934: Röhm and other SA leaders killed, reassuring the army. Hindenburg died in August and Hitler became Führer.
'Coordination': bringing states, unions, the press and clubs under Nazi control.
Stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews.
